scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Imported amboca geometry covers 1492 to 1500 and lies northwest of Loja. Scholarship disagrees about Ambocas distribution and discusses both a population name and colonial province. No exact preconquest border, kingdom or lifespan is certified.

Brito Román’s 2013 anthropology thesis was consulted at the passages cited, not treated as a contemporary colonial eyewitness. Its quotation from Gregorio García distinguishes making adobe blocks from laying them; the public card does not reverse those tasks or reproduce the source’s racist comparison.
The thesis presents Cañari resettlement under Inca rule as an interpretation. No unsupported conquest year or universal Palta ethnic identity is assigned.

Municipal histories provide local narratives with uneven sourcing. The Santiago page’s claim of a first encomendero conflicts with chronologies in scholarship, so that claim is omitted. Its circa 1565 assignment is also present in Brito Román’s table, printed page 111.

The El Cisne account mixes history and devotional tradition. Sculpture commissioning is attributed to the municipal account; the apparition is identified as devotional, not presented as a verified event. No universal precontact diet is taken from modern local crop lists.

Archive entries are finding-aid descriptions. Manuscripts, signatures and handwriting have not been independently examined. Three different documents are cited with box/file or document numbers, and their dates are dates of records rather than community lifetimes.

The 1639 catalog lists leaders and towns without an unambiguous one-to-one mapping, so the public card does not assign an individual signer to a particular town. Allegations of tribute abuse are not recast as independently adjudicated findings.
The Antonio Montoya petition describes alleged imposed stable, household and baking work. Its outcome is unknown from the catalog. This is a concrete labor record, not an archaeological find.
The 1732 rejection concerns one appointment. Later listings include other appointments, so the card does not infer an enduring ban in practice or the disappearance of the colonial province.
Modern FEPROCOL objectives in the thesis include Ambocas heritage. This supports remembrance and reclamation, not an unbroken singular government or a claim about every modern resident’s identity.
No successor link is invented. Independent historical review, geometry verification and depth certification remain pending.
